Kourovka Problem 21.53 asks whether two particular edge colours determine all colours in a graph built from a finite nonabelian simple group. Its vertices form an entire conjugacy class of involutions. The edge joining distinct vertices $a,b$ has colour $|ab|$, the order of their product. If $2,p$ are the two smallest prime divisors of the group order, must every permutation preserving colours $2$ and $p$ preserve every colour? The accepted answer is negative. The theorem [`Kourovka.Problem2153.not_statement`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Final.lean#L14) supplies a counterexample with $p=3$: a transposition preserves colours 2 and 3 but changes an edge from colour 5 to colour 7.

The six custom definitions in [`Core.lean`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Core.lean#L16) make the interpretation explicit. `InvolutionClass` contains every ambient conjugate of the chosen element. `PreservesColour` requires a permutation to carry every edge of a specified colour to that colour; `PreservesAllColours` requires equality of product orders on every distinct pair. `TwoSmallestPrimeDivisors` expresses the divisibility and minimality conditions. `Nonabelian` asks for two noncommuting elements, and `Statement` universally quantifies over the groups, involutions, primes and permutations in the question. These definitions use the ordinary mathlib notions of a group, finiteness, simplicity, conjugacy, element order and permutation. Human statement acceptance covered all six definitions as well as the final theorem.

The counterexample mechanism is short once the group is available. Find conjugate involutions $X,Y,A$ such that

$$
C_G(X)=C_G(Y),\qquad |AX|=5,\qquad |AY|=7,
$$

and such that no product of two members of $X^G$ has order three. Exchange $X$ and $Y$, fixing every other vertex. For distinct involutions, product order two is equivalent to commutation. Equal centralizers therefore give the exchanged vertices identical colour-two neighbours. Colour three is absent altogether. Meanwhile $A$ is fixed, and its edge to $X$ changes colour. [`Endpoint.classSwap`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Endpoint.lean#L20) is exactly this permutation of the whole class.

This makes the main proof obligations visible. The three displayed vertices certify the failure to preserve every colour, but preservation of colours two and three must hold against every other class member. Moreover, the ambient group must satisfy the simplicity hypothesis in the question. The structural part of the formalization proves both requirements, allowing a small witness to answer a universal question about a much larger object.

The group is constructed concretely. [`Field8.F8`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Field8.lean#L15) is an eight-element field whose tables realize $\mathbf F_2[\omega]/(\omega^3+\omega+1)$. Field codes record polynomial coefficients. On its 26-dimensional vector space, explicit invertible matrices $t,x,r,s$, together with 49 diagonal torus matrices, generate [`WilsonModel.ambient`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/WilsonModel.lean#L70). This is an actual subgroup of the standard general linear group, and is finite because the matrix space is finite. The endpoint uses these 26-dimensional matrices. The four-dimensional auxiliary construction elsewhere in the field file does not supply the final ambient group.

The matrices come from Wilson's construction of the Ree groups of type ${}^2F_4$, which credits Coolsaet's earlier Ree–Tits octagon description. The [problem references](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/README.md#references-and-credits) record those sources. The underlying group constructions and simplicity results are prior mathematics. The contribution described here is the explicit whole-class counterexample to Problem 21.53 and its complete formal verification. The required properties are proved directly for the generated matrix group: the argument needs neither recognition as a named Ree group nor an exact group order. Certified elements of orders two and three suffice to show that 2 and 3 are its smallest prime divisors.

Most computation concerns small identities inside this large group. Python-generated data propose sparse matrix products, conjugation formulas and power certificates. Lean proves that the sparse checker agrees with ordinary matrix multiplication, checks the finite data by kernel reduction, and transfers equalities to the actual group through its injective matrix representation. Certificate generation is therefore separate from certificate soundness. A successful external search or a stored numerical answer is not an assumed group-theoretic premise.

To obtain global structure, [`RootSystem.root`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/RootSystem.lean#L42) defines twelve parameterized curves $R_i(a)$ by torus conjugation. Their values generate a subgroup $U$. A curve need not itself be a subgroup: multiplying two values can introduce corrections in later curves. Checked collection relations control those corrections, while torus covariance transports representative identities across field parameters. The decisive consequences are the two factorizations [`U_factor_r` and `U_factor_s`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/UnipotentFactorization.lean#L163),

$$
U=R_rV_r=R_sV_s.
$$

Here $R_r,R_s$ are the respective rank-one subgroups and $V_r,V_s$ are generated by the remaining curves. Commutator relations establish the normalization needed to turn subgroup joins into these products. The endpoint requires neither uniqueness of twelve root coordinates nor enumeration of all $8^{12}$ parameter tuples.

Let $H$ be the torus subgroup, $W=\langle r,s\rangle$, $B=\langle U,H\rangle$, and $N=\langle H,W\rangle$. Sixteen words enumerate $W$. Triangular matrix shapes establish $B\cap N=H$; checked rank-one identities and root-conjugation choices supply the double-coset multiplication rule. With generation and nondegeneracy, these give [`BNPair.concrete`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/BNPair.lean#L9), an actual Tits system. The abstract Bruhat theorem reuses TauCeti at commit `ede1468fb951c5117f1462008216ceb13214e29f`, with its Apache-2.0 license and [source provenance](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/External/TitsSystem/PROVENANCE.json). Every concrete hypothesis is supplied locally. The resulting [`BNPair.uhwu_coverage`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/BNPair.lean#L12) says

$$
g=u h w v\qquad(u,v\in U,\ h\in H,\ w\in W)
$$

for every $g\in G$. This is the bridge from finite representative checks to assertions about the whole group.

The two factorizations explain how the local identities enter that bridge. When multiplying double cosets, they separate a unipotent element into a rank-one factor and a radical factor. The radical moves past the simple reflection. One of 70 checked rank-one identities handles the remaining factor, and the orientation of the Weyl representative determines which positive root factor can be absorbed into the Borel subgroup. These operations establish the abstract multiplication rule on arbitrary elements.

Simplicity is proved through $P=\langle B,r\rangle$ and the abelian subgroup $Z=\langle R_{11}(a)\rangle$. First, $P$ stabilizes a coordinate line, while $s$ moves it, so $P$ is proper. Only containment in the line stabilizer is needed. The [projective-frame certificate](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/AmbientFacts/Frame.lean#L55) gives 27 vectors on orbit lines: 26 form a basis, and the last has no zero coordinate in that basis. An element in the normal core of $P$ fixes all these lines. It is diagonal in the certified basis; the extra line forces all diagonal entries to coincide. Thus it is scalar. Its determinant is one, and $\gcd(26,7)=1$, so that scalar is one. This proves [`P_normalCore`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Parabolic.lean#L81).

Bruhat coverage also proves maximality, in [`P_isCoatom_of_coverage`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/ParabolicMaximal.lean#L27). Any subgroup properly containing $P$ contains a Weyl representative outside $P$. Finite word identities recover the longest Weyl element and then the missing generator $s$, forcing the subgroup to be $G$. Separately, short checked words show that any normal subgroup containing $R_{11}(1)$ contains all ambient generators. Hence [`normalClosure_Z`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/NormalGeneration.lean#L55) says that $Z$ normally generates $G$. A checked commutator places that root element in the derived subgroup, giving [`ambient_perfect`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/NormalGeneration.lean#L61): $G'=G$.

The remaining simplicity argument is elementary. If $K\trianglelefteq G$ lies in $P$, it lies in its trivial core. Otherwise maximality gives $KP=G$. Since $P$ normalizes $Z$, the subgroup $KZ$ is normal in $G$; normal generation forces $KZ=G$. The quotient $G/K$ is consequently an image of the abelian group $Z$. Perfectness makes this quotient trivial. This argument is formalized as [`isSimpleGroup_of_iwasawa_subgroups`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Simplicity.lean#L15); [`ambient_isSimpleGroup`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Simple.lean#L9) applies it with the concrete proofs.

Return now to the three involutions. They are $X=R_{11}(1)$, its torus conjugate $Y=R_{11}(\omega)$, and a Weyl conjugate $A$. [`WilsonModel.witness_orders`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/WilsonModel.lean#L162) proves their exact orders and the exact product orders 5 and 7. Two further finite calculations provide the global conditions. First, 784 Boolean commutation tests show that nonzero last-root elements have the same commuting behaviour against torus–Weyl representatives. Second, the 112 products $X R_{11}(a)^w$, with $a\ne0$, reduce by symmetry to 56 certificates. Each certificate proves a power equal to one, with exponent in $\{1,2,4,5,7,13\}$. These exponent bounds exclude order three; they do not assert an exact order distribution for all 112 products.

Why do these tests suffice? The subgroup $U$ centralizes $Z$. In a decomposition $g=uhwv$, the two unipotent factors therefore disappear from the commutation comparison for $X,Y$. In the product-order comparison, conjugating the product removes them without changing its order. Simultaneous conjugation reduces any pair in $X^G$ to a pair whose first member is $X$. Thus [`Endpoint.same_centralizer_of_coverage`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Endpoint.lean#L65) and [`Endpoint.no_order_three_of_coverage`](../../Kourovka/Problem2153/Endpoint.lean#L72) establish the required statements on the whole group and whole class. The final theorem supplies the proved coverage and simplicity, leaving no structural hypothesis outstanding.
